units.title: Unit 05 — Register
learningObjectives: Select natural collocations for formal, neutral and informal situations without confusing spoken language with informality.
Recognise distinct registers used in journalism, official notices, law, technical descriptions and medical records.
Rephrase informal or specialised expressions into appropriate neutral alternatives while preserving meaning.

items.example: The independent watchdog will look into the deal after receiving several complaints.
items.note: Look into is a neutral phrasal verb for investigating a question or suspected problem.

items.example: An external panel will conduct an investigation into the missing funds.
items.note: Conduct an investigation is more formal than look into a matter.

items.example: The newspaper reported that regulators would probe the agreement.
items.note: Probe is particularly common in concise news reporting and headlines.

items.example: Transactions exceeding the threshold may be subject to investigation by the regulator.
items.note: A formal legal or administrative construction indicating possible scrutiny.

items.example: The journalist managed to dig out information that had been buried in old records.
items.note: Dig out suggests informal, persistent effort to discover difficult-to-find information.

items.pt: um acordo de venda de armas
items.example: Officials declined to comment on the disputed arms deal.
items.note: Arms deal is a conventional noun combination referring to the sale or supply of weapons.

items.example: Every student must submit an assignment through the university portal by Friday.
items.note: Submit an assignment is typical of formal academic instructions and notices.

items.example: Please hand in your assignment before the class ends.
items.note: Hand in is a common neutral alternative to the more formal submit.

items.example: Applicants may request an extension if the required evidence is unavailable.
items.note: Request an extension is formal and appropriate in official or academic correspondence.

items.example: Marta decided to ask for an extension when her laptop stopped working.
items.note: Ask for an extension is a natural neutral way to seek extra time.

items.example: The guidelines recommend that students consult a tutor before changing their topic.
items.note: Consult a tutor sounds more formal than talk to your tutor.

items.word: have a word with your tutor
items.example: You should have a word with your tutor before changing your research question.
items.note: Have a word with someone is conversational and usually means speak briefly.

items.example: The reunion was a blast, and everyone stayed until midnight.
items.note: A blast is informal praise for an enjoyable event or experience.

items.example: The concert was totally awesome, according to the students who attended.
items.note: Totally awesome is enthusiastic and informal, especially in American English.

items.example: My British flatmate said the new restaurant was well good.
items.note: Well meaning very is informal British usage, especially associated with younger speakers.

items.example: I haven't a clue where the spare key has gone.
items.note: Haven't a clue is an informal way of saying that you do not know.

items.pt: não ter a mais vaga ideia
items.example: We haven't the foggiest idea why the alarm went off.
items.note: The foggiest idea intensifies not knowing and is conversational rather than formal.

items.example: We can grab a snack before the afternoon workshop begins.
items.note: Grab a snack sounds informal and suggests eating something quick or convenient.

items.example: The children usually have a snack after swimming lessons.
items.note: Have a snack is a neutral alternative to the more casual grab a snack.

items.example: After a twelve-hour shift, the nurse was dead tired.
items.note: Dead as an intensifier is informal; very tired is more neutral.

items.example: The audience was bored stupid by the repetitive presentation.
items.note: Bored stupid is strongly informal and conveys extreme boredom.

items.example: There is a currency exchange office next to the station entrance.
items.note: A practical and relatively formal term common in travel information and signs.

items.example: The research centre will conduct a study of the new teaching method.
items.note: Conduct a study is an academic and formal equivalent of do a study.

items.example: She plans to do a degree in environmental science next year.
items.note: Do a degree is a natural informal-to-neutral British English academic expression.

items.example: After moving to the city, he managed to find work in a small workshop.
items.note: Find work is neutral language for obtaining employment.

items.example: The laboratory has installed equipment that is bang up to date.
items.note: Bang up to date is emphatic and informal, especially for software or technology.

items.example: Please affix a photograph to the application before submitting it.
items.note: Affix is highly formal language common in instructions and official forms.

items.example: The broadcaster interrupted its schedule to announce breaking news.
items.note: Breaking news is the standard journalism term for a developing important story.

items.example: The band's debut single began to climb the charts after the festival.
items.note: Climb the charts is entertainment-industry language for gaining chart positions.

items.example: There are tons of reasons to learn another language.
items.note: Tons of is an informal way of emphasising a large number.

items.example: Visitors must remain within the designated areas during the tour.
items.note: Designated areas is characteristic of notices and safety instructions.

items.example: A deliberate breach of the policy may cause a claimant to forfeit the right to compensation.
items.note: Forfeit the right is formal legal wording meaning lose an entitlement.

items.example: The vehicle's fuel consumption increased during the mountain journey.
items.note: Fuel consumption is standard technical and automotive terminology.

items.example: I'll give you a ring when I reach the hotel.
items.note: Give someone a ring is informal British English for calling by telephone.

items.word: in a bid to win support
items.pt: em uma tentativa de conquistar apoio
items.example: The minister visited local businesses in a bid to win support for the proposal.
items.note: In a bid to is common in journalism for describing a purposeful attempt.

items.pt: o mais recente grande sucesso de bilheteria
items.example: The cinema added extra screenings of the latest blockbuster.
items.note: Blockbuster is entertainment vocabulary for a very successful big-budget production.

items.example: The sensor incorporates a miniaturised electronic circuit inside its housing.
items.note: Technical phrasing for an electronic circuit made extremely small.

items.example: The notice asks visitors to restrict their use of the computers to thirty minutes.
items.note: Restrict your use of is formal wording often found in public notices.

items.example: The witness agreed to testify in court about the incident.
items.note: Testify in court is conventional legal language for giving evidence formally.

items.example: He was running a temperature and decided to stay home from work.
items.note: Run a temperature is an informal British English expression for having a fever.

items.example: She came out in a rash shortly after trying the new cream.
items.note: Come out in a rash describes suddenly developing a visible skin eruption.

items.example: The pharmacist offered to take a look at the damaged package.
items.note: Take a look is a common informal-to-neutral expression for checking something.

items.word: have trouble getting off to sleep
items.pt: ter dificuldade para pegar no sono
items.example: I have trouble getting off to sleep when I drink coffee late.
items.note: Getting off to sleep means beginning to sleep; the expression is conversational.

items.example: After weeks of travel, the trainer began to feel run down.
items.note: Feel run down describes being tired or lacking energy, often after a demanding period.

items.example: The doctor offered to write out a prescription for the new treatment.
items.note: Write out a prescription is an everyday phrase for preparing a medical prescription.

items.pt: fazer uma erupção na pele desaparecer
items.example: The cream helped clear up a rash that had persisted for days.
items.note: Clear up a rash means cause a skin eruption to disappear or improve.

items.example: Several patients presented with a fever and persistent cough.
items.note: Present with is clinical language describing symptoms observed at consultation.

items.example: The examination revealed an elevated temperature and mild dehydration.
items.note: Elevated temperature is more clinical than saying someone is running a temperature.

items.example: The patient began to exhibit a rash after the second dose.
items.note: Exhibit a rash is relatively technical clinical language describing a visible symptom.

items.word: complain of an inability to concentrate
items.example: Several patients complained of an inability to concentrate after the treatment.
items.note: Complain of is a clinical reporting verb, not necessarily a judgment about the patient.

units.title: Unit 06 — Metaphor
learningObjectives: Understand body-based metaphors for responsibility, leadership, attention, payment and acceptance of reality.
Distinguish weight-related metaphors for serious matters, easy reading, positive feelings and differing degrees of likelihood.
Interpret movement-based idioms accurately, especially contrasts involving quick assumptions and effortless success.

items.example: The audit findings cast light on the reasons for the unexpected delay.
items.note: Cast light on means make a subject easier to understand, not literally illuminate it.

items.example: We must face the facts before proposing another unrealistic deadline.
items.note: Face the facts means accept an uncomfortable reality rather than avoid it.

items.example: The company finally faced up to the facts about its ageing systems.
items.note: Face up to emphasises accepting a difficult truth instead of refusing to acknowledge it.

items.example: Although several people were involved, the manager chose to shoulder the blame.
items.note: Shoulder the blame means accept responsibility for a failure or mistake.

items.example: The organiser agreed to foot the bill for the guests' accommodation.
items.note: Foot the bill means pay the costs, often on behalf of other people.

items.example: An experienced architect will head a team developing the new design.
items.note: Head a team means lead or be in charge of it, not merely support it.

items.pt: manter as pessoas atentas e preparadas
items.example: Unexpected inspections keep people on their toes throughout the season.
items.note: Keep someone on their toes means make them remain alert, active and ready.

items.example: Her ability to spot tiny inconsistencies shows that she has an eye for detail.
items.note: Have an eye for detail means be particularly good at noticing small things.

items.pt: andar de mãos dadas com ou estar associado a
items.example: Rapid growth can go hand in hand with higher operating costs.
items.note: Go hand in hand with means occur together or be closely connected.

items.example: Protecting confidential records is a heavy responsibility for the administrator.
items.note: Heavy describes the seriousness of a responsibility, not physical weight.

items.example: Unpaid debts became a heavy burden for the family.
items.note: A heavy burden may be physical or metaphorical, such as severe responsibility.

items.pt: um livro pesado ou de leitura densa
items.example: I expected a quick read, but the biography turned out to be a heavy book.
items.note: Heavy book can describe either physical weight or difficult, demanding content.

items.example: She spent the holiday studying a weighty tome on medieval philosophy.
items.note: Weighty tome refers to substantial or intellectually demanding reading, not just mass.

items.example: The board met privately to discuss several weighty matters.
items.note: Weighty matters are serious and important, rather than literally heavy.

items.example: The commission must confront weighty problems before changing the rules.
items.note: Weighty problems emphasises seriousness and significant implications.

items.example: On the train, she prefers light reading to demanding academic articles.
items.note: Light reading is entertaining or easy material rather than serious study.

items.example: After receiving the good news, she left the office with a light heart.
items.note: With a light heart suggests relief, happiness or freedom from worry.

items.example: There is a slim chance the missing files can still be recovered.
items.note: A slim chance is small but not necessarily zero.

items.example: Fat chance they'll finish the whole project before lunch!
items.note: Fat chance is very informal and usually ironic, meaning virtually no chance.

items.example: The engineers ran into difficulties during the final installation.
items.note: Run into difficulties means encounter problems and says nothing about speed.

items.example: The residents were hopping mad when the promised repairs were cancelled.
items.note: Hopping mad is a strongly informal way to describe extreme anger.

items.pt: conseguir um emprego com muita facilidade
items.example: With her experience, she walked straight into a job after graduation.
items.note: Walk straight into a job implies finding employment very easily.

items.example: It would be unwise to jump to conclusions before the results are verified.
items.note: Jump to conclusions implies deciding too quickly, often without enough evidence.

items.example: Their partnership hit the rocks after a series of disagreements.
items.note: Hit the rocks describes a relationship or project failing badly, often ending.

items.example: The startup ran into trouble when a key supplier withdrew.
items.note: Run into trouble describes encountering problems, not moving quickly.

items.word: have an eye for a bargain
items.pt: ter olho para boas oportunidades de compra
items.example: My aunt has an eye for a bargain and rarely pays full price.
items.note: An eye for a bargain means an ability to recognise attractive prices or offers.

items.example: Several local firms agreed to back the team through its first season.
items.note: Back a team means support it, whereas head a team means lead it.

items.example: After reviewing the samples, the analysts came to a cautious conclusion.
items.note: Come to a conclusion does not inherently suggest the hasty judgment implied by jump to.

items.example: Don't jump to the wrong conclusion just because one value looks unusual.
items.note: Jump to the wrong conclusion highlights a rapid, mistaken inference.

items.example: She resigned with a heavy heart after many rewarding years.
items.note: With a heavy heart expresses sadness or reluctance, the opposite of a light heart.

items.example: The constant beeping can drive someone crazy during a long shift.
items.note: Drive someone crazy is an idiom for causing intense irritation or frustration.

items.example: The eldest sibling had to shoulder a heavy burden after the family crisis.
items.note: Shoulder a burden combines body and weight metaphors for assuming a difficult duty.

items.example: Reliability continues to head the list of customer priorities.
items.note: Head the list means occupy its first or most important position.
